## My Reasoning

I have been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. Seventy years old now, back a little bent, but I still know the land. My two sons moved to Handan and Shijiazhuang years ago. My wife helps when she can. We have about 10 mu.

There is nothing to decide, really. I grow winter wheat and summer maize. That is what my father grew, what I have always grown. The land here is flat. We have the wells. The supply station sells the inputs. The grain station buys the grain. This is the system. I do not gamble on new crops at my age.

For the wheat, I plant in October after the corn comes off. I hire the rotary tiller machine — I cannot manage the plough myself anymore. I buy improved seed from the village supply station, whatever Jimai variety they have. I apply the diammonium phosphate and potash as base fertilizer, then top-dress urea in late February when the green returns. I irrigate four times: once at sowing to get germination, once in February, once at jointing in April, once more at grain filling in May. I spray herbicide in March, then go out again for the rust and powdery mildew before heading, and once more for aphids. Three sprays is normal here.

For the corn, I plant right after wheat harvest in June — no time to waste. I use 郑单958 hybrid seed, same as everyone in the village. I apply fertilizer as base at planting, top-dress urea once at the big bell stage. If August is dry, I pump water twice. I spray herbicide at emergence and check once more for corn borer. By late September it is done.

I will not change anything this year. My yield is predictable, my costs are known, my body knows the schedule.

Physical limitations and absence of working-age family labour push decisions toward hired mechanised tillage and low-risk conventional inputs purchased from the village supply station. Improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed are the de-facto standard distributed through local channels, so 'improved' and 'hybrid' represent the farmer's normal choice rather than an active innovation.
